text:
Let the Market Park the Cars

Somewhere in your city there's a vacant lot that should hold an apartment building, a bakery, or a small clinic. Often the thing stopping it isn't a lack of money, demand, or ambition. It's a line in the zoning code saying any new building must come with a set number of parking spaces. Cities should delete that line. Minimum parking requirements are among the most expensive and least examined rules in American planning. Removing them is one of the cheapest ways a city can get more housing, better streets, and lower costs.

Start with what these rules do. A typical code says a restaurant needs so many spaces per hundred square feet of dining room, an apartment building needs one or two spaces per unit, and a church needs one space for every few seats. These ratios usually weren't derived from careful study. Many were copied from neighboring towns or from guidance written decades ago, when planners assumed every trip would be made by car and that running out of curb space was the worst thing that could happen to a neighborhood. The UCLA planner Donald Shoup, whose book "The High Cost of Free Parking" made this case almost twenty years ago, compared the process to astrology: the numbers carry the authority of precision without the substance.

The costs are real, and somebody pays them. A space in an above-ground garage can cost tens of thousands of dollars to build, and an underground space can cost far more. Those costs go into rents, mortgages, and the price of a sandwich, whether or not the person paying owns a car. A household without a car, which is often a household with less money, subsidizes the parking of people who drive. On small or odd-shaped lots, the requirement can make a project unworkable outright. The ramps, turning radii, and stall dimensions eat the site, and the apartment building that would have fit simply doesn't get built. Nobody holds a press conference for housing that was never proposed, so this cost stays out of sight.

The rules also shape what our places look like. Mandated parking is why so many commercial strips are a building marooned in a sea of asphalt, set back from the sidewalk behind rows of stalls that sit half empty most of the year. It pushes buildings apart, which lengthens every walk and makes transit less useful, which in turn makes people more dependent on cars. The requirement creates the car-oriented city it claims merely to accommodate.

Opponents raise a fair worry: if developers don't have to build parking, won't residents and customers flood the streets looking for spaces? This deserves a direct answer, not a dismissal. First, removing a minimum isn't a ban. Developers who think their tenants or shoppers need parking will still build it, because lenders, buyers, and retailers will insist on it. Abolishing the mandate lets the amount of parking follow actual demand instead of a guess written into law. In practice, developers in cities that have dropped minimums keep building parking, just less of it and in places where it makes sense. Second, the right tool for crowded curbs is managing the curb: residential permit zones, meters priced to keep a few spaces open on each block, and time limits enforced consistently. Those tools work on the street where the problem is. A parking minimum works on a building that hasn't been built yet, and it does so crudely.

The places that have tried this aren't fringe experiments. Buffalo eliminated parking minimums citywide in 2017. Minneapolis followed in 2021, and San Jose, Austin, and others have done the same since. California passed a state law in 2022 barring cities from imposing minimums on most development near major transit. The results haven't been chaos. What they show is projects on lots that couldn't previously pencil out, conversions of old buildings that had been stuck because they had nowhere to add spaces, and developers choosing parking ratios that fit their tenants rather than the code.

There's also a simpler argument about fairness and honesty in government. A city that wants more affordable housing while requiring every new unit to come with an expensive concrete stall is working against itself. A city that says it wants fewer car trips while mandating free storage for cars at every destination is sending contradictory signals. Getting rid of parking minimums doesn't force anyone out of their car. It stops forcing everyone else to pay for one.

None of this means parking doesn't matter. It matters a great deal, which is exactly why decisions about it should be made by the people who know their own buildings and customers, backed by smart management of public streets, rather than by a ratio someone set in 1965. Cities should repeal their parking minimums, fix their curb policies, and let the asphalt shrink to the size we actually need. The vacant lot is waiting.
